Aftereffect direction could not be settled from the paper's wording: Fig. 1 plots signed angular errors on an axis extending to negative values and the text only says the after-effect was 'similar in both age groups', so higher_is_better is 'unknown'. Dataset 2: all control-sample tracking values live only in Fig. 2 (page 4, thin lines); the Fig. 2 caption never states what the plotted bars represent, so error_bar_type is UNKNOWN with no evidence quote. No after-effect phase exists for the control sample ('five tracking episodes with +60° rotated feedback on the second day' only), so no aftereffect outcome is listed for dataset 2. outcomes.measure_name: Angular pointing error (median initial direction error per episode)
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: Their errors increased abruptly at the onset of the adaptation phase, and then gradually dropped again. Most importantly, adaptive improvement was more pronounced for young than for old subjects.
outcomes.operationalization: Median initial movement direction error (between movement onset and peak velocity) per 50-s episode, averaged across subjects, during the 15 pointing episodes with +60° rotated visual feedback (episodes 6–20 in Fig. 1); the end of the adaptation phase is the last adaptation episode (episode 20). An alternative operationalization printed in the text is the asymptote of the exponential fit to the adaptation time course for each age group.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, adaptation phase (filled symbols, pointing episodes 6–20); last adaptation episode (episode 20); triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: Fig. 1 Mean pointing errors of young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects before, during, and after exposure to rotated visual feedback. Open symbols indicate episodes where visual feedback was absent. Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.sample_note: Caption names both age groups: "young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects"; these are the 12+12 experimental subjects of the pointing task.
sources.notes: Only source that plots the group means with dispersion for the adaptation phase; no numeric adaptation-episode values are printed in the text. Filled symbols = feedback present (adaptation and refresh phases).

sources.locator: Results, end of first paragraph on the adaptation phase (exponential fit equations for each age group)
sources.quote: An exponential fit yielded y=9.92+53.51×exp(−x/5.89) for young subjects and y=29.51+29.91×exp(−x/5.13) for old subjects.
sources.sample_note: "for young subjects" and "for old subjects" — the two age groups of the pointing experiment, fitted separately.
sources.notes: Fitted-model parameters (asymptote, amplitude, time constant) of the adaptation time course; the asymptote (9.92 young, 29.51 old) is a second operationalization of late adaptation. No dispersion or fit error reported; a human must decide whether to use the asymptote or the Fig. 1 episode-20 means.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA on the adaptation phase (between-factor Age, within-factor Episode)
sources.quote: We confirmed these observations by analysis of variance (ANOVA) for the adaptation phase, using the between-factor Age and the within-factor Episode: significant effects were yielded for Age (F(1,22)=7.58, P<0.05), Episode (F(14,308)=41.14, P<0.001), and their interaction (F(14,308)=3.44, P<0.001).
sources.sample_note: Between-factor Age (young vs old), 12 per group (df 1,22).
sources.notes: Mixed ANOVA: the Age main effect is computed on angular errors averaged over all 15 adaptation episodes, not on the end of the adaptation phase, and p is bounded (P<0.05); therefore context, not a value source. Interaction and Episode effects are within-subject/interaction terms.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, baseline phases (episodes 1–3 pointing without feedback, open symbols; episodes 4–5 pointing with veridical feedback, filled symbols), triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: Both age groups pointed quite accurately during the two baseline phases without and with visual feedback.
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.sample_note: Same two age groups plotted across the whole session in Fig. 1.
sources.notes: Pre-perturbation baseline pointing errors that could be used to baseline-correct the adaptation values; not the outcome itself.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA on the refresh phase and on episodes 20 vs 26
sources.quote: Accordingly, ANOVA yielded significant effects of Age (F(1,22)=13.42, P<0.01) and Episode (F(2,44)=6.18, P<0.01), but no significant interaction. ... we compared the pointing errors in episodes 20 and 26 by an additional ANOVA; the effects of Age (F(1,22)=13.78, P<0.01) and Episode (F(1,22)=7.79, P<0.05)
sources.notes: These tests concern the post-break refresh phase (episodes 26–28) and a comparison of episode 20 with episode 26, i.e. a second round of rotated feedback; outside the protocol's initial-adaptation window and with bounded p values. Context only.

sources.locator: Results, pooled-seniors correlation analysis (adaptation magnitude A after 12.5 min of exposure)
sources.quote: In effect, our sample size thus increased to 54 seniors aged 64.0±4.5 years, all healthy and naïve to the experiment. The magnitude of adaptation in this sample was 0.49±0.21, and the normalized trail-making score was 1.78±0.55.
sources.error_bar_evidence: twelve young (26.0±5.0 years of age) and twelve older (69.5±7.5 years of age) subjects
sources.values_in_text: adaptation magnitude 0.49±0.21 (54 seniors); normalized trail-making score 1.78±0.55
sources.sample_note: "our sample size thus increased to 54 seniors" — seniors of this study pooled with seniors from two previous, unpublished experiments; no matching young-group value is given.
sources.notes: Adaptation magnitude A=(I−F)/I, a proportional-improvement index, reported for a pooled seniors sample only (not for the 12 young subjects of this dataset), so it cannot serve as the group contrast; dispersion sign convention (±) assumed to be SD as elsewhere in the paper.

outcomes.measure_name: Angular pointing error during no-feedback after-effect episodes
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: Further, from Fig. 1, when visual feedback was removed after adaptation, the resulting after-effect was similar in both age groups, and gradually declined with practice
outcomes.operationalization: Median initial pointing direction error per 50-s episode during the five after-effect episodes of pointing without visual feedback that immediately followed the 15 adaptation episodes (open symbols after episode 20 in Fig. 1); the first of these episodes (episode 21) is the first available measure of the post-learning phase.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, after-effect phase (open symbols following pointing episode 20, i.e. episodes 21–25); first after-effect episode; triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: Open symbols indicate episodes where visual feedback was absent. Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.sample_note: Caption: "young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects" — the 12+12 experimental subjects of the pointing task.
sources.notes: The only location plotting after-effect means with SD; no numeric after-effect values are printed in the text. The y axis of Fig. 1 extends to negative values (labelled down to −40), so the plotted after-effect errors are signed and the sign convention must be settled by a human before reading.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA on the after-effect phase
sources.quote: ANOVA yielded significant effects for Episode (F(4,88)=66.84, P<0.001) and the interaction (F(4,88)=3.95, P<0.01); indeed a close look at Fig. 1 reveals that the after-effect declined somewhat faster in the young group.
sources.sample_note: Same mixed design with between-factor Age (young, old) and within-factor Episode as used for the adaptation phase.
sources.notes: Only the within-subject Episode main effect and the Age×Episode interaction are reported; no Age main effect statistic is printed for the after-effect phase, so nothing here is a value source for the group contrast.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, baseline pointing without visual feedback (open symbols, episodes 1–3), triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: Next came three baseline episodes of pointing without visual feedback, followed by ten baseline episodes of tracking with veridical feedback.
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.sample_note: Both age groups plotted in Fig. 1 across the whole session.
sources.notes: No-feedback baseline (same feedback condition as the after-effect phase); usable to baseline-correct the after-effect values. Quote of the methods description is on page 2; the plotted points are in Fig. 1 on page 3.

outcomes.measure_name: Tracking error, root mean square error between target and cursor (RMSE)
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: Clearly, tracking errors were higher during visual rotation; this increase was substantial in control subjects, and was followed by a gradual improvement, particularly for young participants.
outcomes.operationalization: RMSE between target and cursor per 50-s tracking episode (initial 0.5 s excluded), for the control subjects who were not pre-adapted with pointing, during the five tracking episodes with +60° rotated feedback on the second day (thin lines, episodes 11–15 in Fig. 2); the end of this block is the last rotated episode (episode 15).

sources.locator: Fig. 2, thin lines (control subjects), rotated-feedback episodes 11–15; last rotated episode; triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: Fig. 2 Mean tracking errors of young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects before and during exposure to rotated visual feedback. Bold lines represent experimental subjects which adapted to the rotation in a pointing task before being transferred to tracking; thin lines represent control subjects not pre-adapted with pointing
sources.sample_note: Caption: "young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects ... thin lines represent control subjects not pre-adapted with pointing" — the 12 young and 12 old control volunteers.
sources.notes: Only location with group RMSE values for the control sample; no numeric tracking RMSE is printed anywhere in the text. The Fig. 2 caption does not state what the plotted vertical bars are (unlike Fig. 1), so the dispersion type is unknown. Note the x axis of Fig. 2 is printed as "pointing episode".

sources.locator: Fig. 2, thin lines (control subjects), baseline tracking episodes 1–10 with veridical feedback; triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: Those subjects only executed ten tracking episodes with veridical feedback on the first day and five tracking episodes with +60° rotated feedback on the second day.
sources.sample_note: Control subjects: "additional twelve young (22.6±1.9 years of age) and twelve old (72.5±6.0 years of age) healthy and naïve volunteers".
sources.notes: Veridical-feedback baseline tracking curve plotted beside the rotated curve; the quoted methods sentence describing these episodes is on page 3, while the plotted points are in Fig. 2 on page 4.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA on above-baseline tracking error (between-factors Age and Procedure)
sources.quote: We therefore calculated each subject's above-baseline error as the difference between the RMSE in episode 11, and the mean RMSE in episode 6–10, and submitted the outcome to an ANOVA with the between-factors Age (young, old) and Procedure (experimental, control). Only the effect of Procedure was significant (F(1,43)=144,09, P<0.001).
sources.sample_note: "between-factors Age (young, old) and Procedure (experimental, control)" — all four subgroups (experimental and control, young and old) analysed together, df 1,43.
sources.notes: Reported effect is the Procedure main effect (experimental vs control, collapsing age), computed on the first rotated tracking episode minus the mean of baseline episodes 6–10; no Age main effect statistic or group means are printed. Also defines the above-baseline (change-from-baseline) operationalization used for the transfer test.
